Με κέντρο τον Ραχμάνινοφ

The Megaron Mousikis hall settles into focused silence as the orchestra takes position. The program tonight centers on Rachmaninoff — that particular Russian romantic sensibility, the piano writing that demands everything from a performer, the orchestral textures that feel like weather systems moving through the concert hall.

Centering an evening on Rachmaninoff means committing to emotional architecture. His compositions don't do restraint. The piano concertos require virtuosity, but the real challenge is sustaining the emotional arc across movements that span vast territory. The Megaron's programming places his work in context, surrounded by complementary pieces that illuminate different facets of the repertoire.

The audience for classical music at Megaron brings particular expectations. These are listeners who've heard these pieces before — many times, many interpretations — and come specifically to experience this version, these performers, this evening. Scores sometimes appear on laps. Eyes close during familiar passages. The attention is intense in the way that only classical music audiences achieve.

The Megaron Mousikis provides the acoustic environment Rachmaninoff requires. Built for orchestral precision, the hall amplifies the quietest passages while handling the biggest climaxes without strain. When the piano cascades through a particularly demanding passage, the room contains the sound without collapsing it. When the orchestra swells to Rachmaninoff's characteristic peaks, the experience becomes physical.

If you want music that provides background atmosphere, that asks nothing of its listeners, this program will overwhelm you. Rachmaninoff wrote for active attention — the structures reveal themselves to those who follow them. But if you're ready to give yourself to an evening of Russian romantic piano music performed in one of Europe's finest concert halls — if you want to hear why Rachmaninoff still packs these rooms — you're in the right seats.

At the center of tonight's program: the composer who wrote for every emotion simultaneously.

MIRANDA VEROULI QUINTET - GAL COSTA MUSA TROPICAL

You settle into a candlelit table as the first notes of a Brazilian guitar fill the room. The warmth of bossa nova wraps around you while the scent of wine mingles with the low hum of conversation. This is where Athens comes to remember that music can be both sophisticated and sensual.

Miranda Verouli leads her quintet through a tribute to Gal Costa, the Brazilian singer whose voice defined tropicália and MPB for five decades. Costa's catalog—from the psychedelic experimentation of the late 1960s to the romantic ballads that made her a household name—gets reimagined for an intimate jazz club setting.

The crowd here knows their music. You'll find vinyl collectors who can debate the relative merits of Costa's Tropicália albums, couples who slow-danced to these songs in their youth, and younger listeners discovering this repertoire for the first time. Nobody's checking their phone.

| Aspect | Details | |--------|---------| | **Setting** | Intimate jazz club, ~150 capacity, low ceilings amplify every note | | **Vibe** | Warm, romantic, conversational | | **Sound** | Listening room—every brush on the snare audible | | **Seating** | Tables with full service, bar stools for solo visitors |

The set builds from quiet acoustic arrangements through to the full-blooded samba that Costa made her own. Expect the quintet to find new angles on familiar melodies.

If you want loud or want to dance—this isn't it. But if you're the kind of person who listens to albums start to finish and appreciates musicians who've studied their craft for decades, pull up a chair.

Half Note is where Athens' serious jazz listeners have gathered since 1979. For Brazilian jazz, there's nowhere else in the city with this combination of sound quality and atmosphere.
